analysis.one_liner: Repeals the mandated transfer of the sacred Oak Flat site in Arizona's Tonto National Forest to a mining company.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had a Democratic lead sponsor and three Republican cosponsors, never received a vote and died in committee at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2014 defense bill required the Forest Service to hand over about 2,422 acres of public land known as Oak Flat to Resolution Copper Mining in exchange for private parcels elsewhere. Oak Flat is sacred to Apache and other Tribal nations and sits above a massive copper deposit the company plans to mine using a method that would collapse the surface. This bill would cancel that transfer, keeping Oak Flat in public hands.
analysis.who_benefits: San Carlos Apache and other Tribal nations for whom Oak Flat is a sacred ceremonial site, plus campers, climbers, hunters, and other public-lands users in Arizona, and anyone in the region concerned about the aquifer and water supplies beneath the site.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tribal nations and Arizona public-lands users

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the provision in the 2015 defense authorization act that requires the Agriculture Department to convey roughly 2,422 acres of Forest Service land in Pinal County, Arizona, to Resolution Copper Mining in exchange for the company's private parcels [S2].

The bill's findings state that Oak Flat is sacred to regional Indian Tribes, is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and that the planned block-cave mining method would cause the surface to subside and collapse, permanently destroying the sacred area [S3].
The findings also state the mining project would deplete and contaminate water resources and that polluted water could seep into drinking water supplies [S3].
The findings say the 2014 land-transfer provision was added to the defense bill without majority support in either chamber and without allowing a vote on an amendment to remove it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Resolution Copper, a joint venture of the mining companies Rio Tinto and BHP, would lose title to the land it was set to receive, and the country would forgo a large new domestic copper supply along with the mine's jobs and investment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Resolution Copper and its mining-company parents

drawbacks.text: Repealing the provision cancels the exchange in which Resolution Copper would have conveyed its own private land parcels to the federal government, ending that conservation trade [S2].

Oak Flat sits above one of the largest known untapped copper deposits in North America, and copper is a basic input for wiring, electrification, and defense hardware, so blocking the mine forgoes a significant domestic supply of a strategic mineral at some cost to manufacturing and energy buildout (this is how the copper-supply mechanism works, not something the provided sources quantify).

If the mine had proceeded under normal land-management and environmental review, it could have brought jobs and investment to a rural Arizona county; the bill forecloses that development path entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a large domestic copper supply and the mine's economic activity for the protection of a sacred Tribal site, a unique recreation area, and the aquifer beneath it. The transfer it would repeal was itself attached to a must-pass defense bill without a standalone vote or allowed amendment, so the choice Congress faced was not between this project and a full public review but between keeping and undoing an exchange that never received one. The environmental and religious-liberty costs are permanent and land-based; the copper supply, while real, can be developed only by destroying the site.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Natural Resources Committee and then to two subcommittees, and it sat there without a markup or floor vote until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the Save Oak Flat Act on January 17, 2019, with 30 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day [S3] [S5].

On February 8, 2019, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee for Indigenous Peoples of the United States and the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands; it received no further action [S5].
By the end of the Congress the bill had 39 cosponsors, 36 of the chamber's 231 Democrats and 3 of its 197 Republicans [S4].
Because the repeal never passed, the underlying 2014 requirement to convey Oak Flat to Resolution Copper remained on the books, and the 2,422-acre exchange stayed authorized by law [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Resolution Copper and its parent mining companies are better off, because the 2014 law requiring the transfer of Oak Flat to them stayed in effect, and Tribal nations and public-lands users lost their one vehicle in this Congress to stop it. The land-transfer law ultimately took effect after this Congress ended, when the Forest Service completed the process and the transfer went through in January 2021 — a widely reported event outside the provided sources.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Resolution Copper and its mining-company parents

for.role: Tribal governments opposing the Oak Flat transfer

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or advanced the bill after referring it to two subcommittees on February 8, 2019; it received no further action for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Resolution Copper (Rio Tinto / BHP joint venture)
against.role: Mining company set to receive Oak Flat

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was mostly Democratic — 36 of 231 Democrats versus 3 of 197 Republicans — though the Republican cosponsors show some crossover; no votes occurred, so the split was never tested on the floor.

industries.industry: Copper mining (Resolution Copper — Rio Tinto/BHP joint venture)
industries.note: The bill would cancel the transfer of 2,422 acres of public land the company needs for a mine whose block-cave method would collapse the surface of a sacred site, per the bill's own findings. Its gain under existing law comes at the direct cost of Tribal religious practice and the region's water [S3].

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation and tourism businesses near Oak Flat (camping, climbing, guided outings)
industries.note: Keeping Oak Flat in public hands preserves a recreation area that a collapsing mine pit would destroy. The site is used by the public under Forest Service management.
